classification.tone: Heightened, sexually frank, literary, comic, and emotionally bruised

evaluation.positioning_hook: A Houston twentysomething juggles bar hookups, art ambition, and family pressure as one chaotic month turns desire into identity.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The script has a clear, contemporary audience lane: sexually charged relationship comedy with a strong Houston-specific identity, music culture, and art-world aspiration. The month-by-month structure gives it an accessible romantic engine, while the bar banter, family dynamics, and public-facing creative careers broaden the appeal beyond a single couple.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The premise lands quickly through the January-to-April progression, with Taryn and Carter’s relationship, Ali’s art competition, and the family/industry pressure all introduced early. The script’s engine is easy to track: a group of young adults chasing love, status, and self-definition while their lives keep colliding.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Taryn, Carter, Ali, Riley, and Joshua each have a distinct social rhythm, and the script gives them memorable contradictions: Carter is goofy but performatively intellectual, Taryn is insecure but sharp, Ali is tender but prideful, Riley is socially fluent, Joshua is charming until he isn’t. The central quartet has enough chemistry and friction to carry a feature and suggest a larger world around them.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script takes real swings: literary voiceover, chaptered time jumps, art-world satire, Houston specificity, and a tonal blend that moves from raunchy comedy to menace to sincerity. The choice to build a feature around young creatives, audiobook culture, and a very specific social ecosystem gives it a confident, authored feel.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The story keeps generating fresh situations—escape room, art competition, blood donation, house parties, studio sessions, the gala, the chase—so the read stays active and eventful. The back half especially benefits from the Joshua thread, which adds suspense and gives the romantic/ensemble material a sharper edge.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The script feels like it knows exactly what it is: a Houston relationship comedy where art, class, race, and commitment are all part of the same social game. The combination of literary narration, local texture, and a very specific young-adult milieu creates the “of course this exists” quality that makes a script feel discoverable.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: Houston is not just backdrop here; the bars, Montrose apartments, Menil, real estate culture, family restaurant, and local social codes all create a lived-in ecosystem. The script also uses creative subcultures—bartending, audiobook narration, painting, music-making, real estate—to make the world feel like a network of adjacent hustles.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The tone is unusually specific: horny, literary, self-aware, and emotionally sincere without ever becoming precious. Scenes like the bar flirtation, the art-world confrontation, the blood-truck sequence, and the final musical declaration all belong to the same tonal universe, which is a strong sign of control.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Under the comedy, the script keeps revealing deeper material about abandonment, identity, cultural performance, and the fear of choosing a life too early. Taryn’s audiobook work, Carter’s grief, Ali’s trauma, and Joshua’s fixation all suggest a richer interior life than the surface banter initially advertises.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: The script is built on a web rather than a single pair: Taryn/Carter, Taryn/Riley, Carter/Ali, Ali/Joshua, Taryn/Evelyn, Evelyn/Tender, and the family dynamics all generate story. The best scenes come from combinations of characters in rooms together, which is exactly what gives the feature its social propulsion.

casting_characteristics: Late-20s/early-30s ensemble with strong chemistry requirements
Musical performance ability helpful for Carter, Taryn, and Tender
Actor with strong comic timing needed for Joshua

locations.interior_exterior_ratio: Mostly interior with frequent exterior transitions
notable_requirements: Houston-area bars, homes, art spaces, and upscale restaurant locations
High school exterior and parking lot

technical.vfx_details: Primarily title/time transitions, aspect-ratio shifts for TV inserts, and a few stylized flashback/transition moments
technical.sfx_needs: Practical blood effects for the party-store accident and hospital aftermath; car impact sequence at the high school; plastic-wrap bondage setup; stage-style musical number staging

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model with strong festival-to-platform potential; the social, sexual, and musical material is best suited to a streamer or specialty distributor

strengths.what_it_means: The script has a real sense of place, and that makes it instantly ownable. The bars, Montrose apartments, Menil, Greenway Plaza, Westheimer, and the family restaurant all create a local ecosystem that feels lived-in rather than generic, which is valuable both creatively and commercially.
strengths.evidence: The story repeatedly grounds itself in Houston neighborhoods, institutions, and social spaces, from Bar Charlar to the Menil Collection to the Albion at Sunset.

strengths.what_it_means: This is built for actors. Carter, Taryn, Ali, and Riley all have distinct comic and emotional registers, and the script keeps pairing them in ways that generate fresh friction and flirtation. That gives the movie a social engine, not just a plot engine.
strengths.evidence: The bar flirtation, the art competition bet, the blood-donation detour, and the party-store sequence all depend on character interplay.

strengths.what_it_means: The script can pivot from raunchy comedy to emotional vulnerability to menace without feeling random. That tonal confidence is a selling point because it suggests a filmmaker with a clear point of view and gives the project a distinctive trailer language.
strengths.evidence: The script moves from nipple-buttering jokes to literary narration to Joshua’s captivity sequence to the final romantic musical number.

strengths.what_it_means: At its core, this is a relationship movie about two people who are clearly drawn to each other but keep getting in their own way. That’s a durable, actor-friendly engine with broad emotional accessibility.
strengths.evidence: Carter and Taryn’s flirtation, jealousy, breakup, reconciliation, and final public declaration structure the feature.

strengths.what_it_means: The script has a sharp, funny eye for how art, taste, and status get performed. That gives the movie a smart, elevated texture and opens the door to a more sophisticated audience than a standard rom-com.
strengths.evidence: The escape-room symphony, the art competition, the Menil backstory, the dealer pitch, and the final gallery-style confrontations all play into this world.

strengths.what_it_means: Music is not decorative here; it’s part of the storytelling DNA. Between the audiobook narration, the rap references, the album release, and the final duet, the script has a built-in soundtrack identity that can help marketing and audience memory.
strengths.evidence: Tender’s album Vows, Carter’s final serenade, and the recurring use of music and voice as identity markers.

strengths.what_it_means: The leads are written with enough specificity to attract talent looking for a showcase: comic timing, emotional vulnerability, seduction, shame, and public performance all live in the same parts.
strengths.evidence: Taryn’s audiobook work, Carter’s performative charm, Ali’s wounded pride, and Joshua’s volatile charisma each give an actor something playable.

strengths.what_it_means: The script is structured around memorable, filmable moments that can anchor a trailer and help the movie feel eventful: the escape room, the blood-truck accident, the art expo confrontation, the musical proposal, and the airport chase.
strengths.evidence: Each of these sequences is distinct in location, tone, and visual identity.

whats_special.headline: This is a smart, sexy Houston ensemble piece with a real voice: part romantic comedy, part art-world satire, part coming-of-age story. The script’s biggest asset is how confidently it turns local texture, sharp dialogue, and emotionally messy relationships into a movie that feels both commercial and authored.

lead_characters.name: Taryn Reese
lead_characters.hook: Taryn is the kind of heroine who looks polished before she feels settled. She’s a voice performer, a real estate agent, a daughter, a sister, and a woman who keeps trying on identities until one finally fits. Under the makeup and flirtation is a sharp, self-conscious intelligence; she notices everything, wants to be chosen, and is quietly terrified that she’s only ever the supporting character in other people’s lives. Her emotional life is built around longing, comparison, and the need to matter.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a rich, contemporary lead role with range: comedy, sensuality, insecurity, romantic yearning, and a late-script emotional reckoning. It gives an actor the chance to be funny and vulnerable in the same breath, with a final stretch that asks for real interiority. The part sits in the lane of performances like Greta Gerwig in Frances Ha or Rachel Sennott in Shiva Baby, where wit and self-exposure are the engine.

lead_characters.name: Carter Pusset
lead_characters.hook: Carter is a charming improviser who treats life like a performance he can win if he stays loose enough. He’s flirtatious, goofy, and socially gifted, but the script keeps revealing the seriousness underneath the swagger: grief, fear of commitment, and a deep need to be seen as more than a pretty face behind a bar. He’s the rare rom-com lead who can talk his way into a room and still feel emotionally unfinished when he gets there.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a star-making kind of part because it asks for charisma first and self-awareness second. Carter gets the banter, the swagger, the romantic lift, and the emotional collapse, plus a final act that lets an actor play public declaration and private damage at once. The role has the kind of tonal breadth that rewards someone in the space of Glen Powell in Hit Man or Paul Mescal in Aftersun when the script wants charm with ache.

lead_characters.name: Ali Khalid
lead_characters.hook: Ali is the most quietly wounded person in the room, which makes him the emotional ballast of the movie. He’s an artist with discipline, pride, and a real sense of purpose, but he’s also carrying humiliation, abandonment, and a need to prove he’s not the joke in someone else’s story. The script gives him a beautiful contradiction: he is both the most serious and the most vulnerable guy in the group, and that tension makes him deeply watchable.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a prestige-supporting-to-lead caliber role for an actor who wants to play hurt without losing dignity. The captivity sequence, the basketball flashback, and the art-world material give him a lot of emotional and physical terrain, while the friendship scenes let him play dry comedy and wounded pride. It has the same kind of showcase energy as Riz Ahmed in Sound of Metal or LaKeith Stanfield in Sorry to Bother You when the character is both funny and haunted.

lead_characters.name: Riley Thomas
lead_characters.hook: Riley is the social strategist of the group: quick, observant, and always half a step ahead of the room. She has the easy confidence of someone who knows how to close a sale and the emotional intelligence to read a situation before anyone else names it. What makes her pop is that she’s not just the funny friend; she’s the one who understands the mechanics of desire, presentation, and persuasion better than anyone else in the story.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: Riley is a scene-stealing role with real utility: she can drive dialogue, land comic beats, and still carry emotional subtext. The blood-donation sequence and the real-estate scenes show how naturally she can command a room, which makes this a strong part for an actor who wants a smart, modern supporting lead in the spirit of Ayo Edebiri in The Bear or Zoë Kravitz in High Fidelity.

lead_characters.name: Joshua Cohen
lead_characters.hook: Joshua starts as the funny, slightly odd bartender with a spiritual streak and then reveals himself as the movie’s most volatile presence. He’s wounded, performative, and deeply funny until he isn’t, which gives him a dangerous unpredictability that keeps the audience leaning in. The character is built on contradiction: he wants connection, but he weaponizes intimacy the moment he feels exposed.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of supporting role that can steal the movie. Joshua gets the comic material, the menace, the captivity monologue, and the final reveal, all of which give an actor a chance to pivot from charm to threat in a way that’s memorable. It has the energy of a Jesse Plemons or Lakeith Stanfield-type turn where the audience can’t quite decide whether to laugh or back away.

lead_characters.name: Tender
lead_characters.hook: Tender is a polished public figure who understands branding, romance, and emotional theater as part of the same package. He’s gracious, controlled, and commercially savvy, but the script lets him reveal a real emotional intelligence beneath the celebrity sheen. He functions as both a romantic ideal and a mirror for the story’s obsession with performance.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a sleek, high-status supporting role with music-world cachet and real charisma. It gives an actor the chance to play a famous man who is still legible as human, especially in the dinner-table scenes and the album-launch sequence. The part has the kind of smooth, controlled presence that could attract someone in the space of Donald Glover in Atlanta or Yahya Abdul-Mateen II when the role needs elegance with edge.

considerations.detail: This plays in a mid-budget feature lane, with most of the spend concentrated in cast, music, nightlife, and a handful of set-piece sequences rather than large-scale spectacle.
The script uses a large number of named songs, artists, and cultural references, and the final musical sequence makes music rights and soundtrack strategy central to packaging.
The project benefits from actors with strong comic timing, natural chemistry, and comfort with heightened dialogue; the ensemble is a major part of the movie’s appeal.
This is best positioned for viewers who respond to relationship-driven, sexually frank, culturally specific contemporary stories with a strong voice and a little edge.
The script’s blend of raunch, sincerity, literary narration, and menace creates a distinctive identity that would be well served by a filmmaker with a confident tonal hand.
The material feels especially suited to a festival launch or streamer-first rollout, where the voice, cast, and cultural specificity can be highlighted quickly.
